prompt:
You review an organisation's governed process documents for knowledge-governance issues.
You are given two statements, each from a different document or section. Classify their relationship:
- "conflict": they cannot both be followed or both be true for the same subject, scope and time, for example
  different values, owners, order of steps or methods, or one requires what the other rules out.
- "duplicate": they give the same substantive guidance, so one could replace the other.
- "neither": anything else: they are about different subjects, processes, item types, phases, sites or dates;
  one is an exception to, or a later phase of, the other; or they add different, compatible information.
Judge only what the statements say. Different wording alone is not a conflict.
Return JSON: {"relation": "conflict" | "duplicate" | "neither", "reason": "<one sentence>"}

audit.method: system prompt + one user message with the two statements; JSON parsed from the reply
audit.sent: the pre-registered system prompt and, per case, the two statements (document title, section heading, text) from tests/evaluation/governance_pair_benchmark.json

rows.reason: Statement A requires due diligence and credit checks to be completed before supplier activation (gating controls), while Statement B permits them to be completed after activation, directly contradicting the sequencing and gate status of these controls.

Statement A requires all three contracts (commercial, service, and payment) before a supplier can be used in downstream processes, while Statement B permits using a supplier with only a commercial contract, making service and payment contracts optional.

Statement A assigns due diligence and credit checks to the accounts payable/offshore support team, while Statement B assigns the same checks to the buyer/commercial requester and explicitly excludes accounts payable involvement, creating mutually exclusive role responsibilities for the same process.

Statement A asserts that creating a supplier header record does NOT mean the supplier is ready for operational use, while Statement B asserts that once the header record is created, the supplier IS ready for operational use—these are directly contradictory positions on the same subject.
Statement A advocates for automated supplier numbering to reduce duplication risk, while Statement B explicitly prohibits automated numbering and requires manual assignment by the operator.

Statement A requires articles to be linked at the lowest operational level of the merchandise hierarchy, while Statement B explicitly permits linking at any level and states the lowest level is not required.

Statement A says an active and published article is not automatically sellable at site level, while Statement B says an article becomes sellable at every site as soon as it is active and published downstream, which directly contradicts the conditional nature in Statement A.

The statements prescribe opposite methods for handling general tax-rate changes: Statement A requires closing the old definition and opening a new one, while Statement B requires editing the existing definition in place.
Statement A requires removal of items that no longer meet criteria at the next refresh, while Statement B requires items to remain permanently on automatic lists regardless of criteria changes.

Statement A requires pack-size changes to follow a dedicated product-change process rather than simple overwrite, while Statement B explicitly permits pack-size changes to be overwritten directly in the article record.

Statement A requires legacy article numbers to remain aligned with target records during dual maintenance until legacy environment retirement, while Statement B permits discontinuing this alignment once the target record exists, directly contradicting the maintenance requirement.

Statement A specifies mass maintenance for day-one assortment upload while Statement B specifies direct live integration from the planning system, and both explicitly exclude the other method for the same day-one scenario.

Statement A prescribes full extract reloads as preferable during earliest cutover stages, while Statement B mandates delta loads must be used instead during the same phase, creating incompatible requirements for the same process and timeframe.
The two statements specify different acknowledgment timeframes (2 working days vs. 5 working days) for the same action by the same team on the same subject.

Statement A states the national price list applies only as a fallback when no more specific list overrides it, while Statement B states the national price list always takes priority over more specific lists, making them mutually exclusive in their governance of price list precedence.

Statement A requires that priorities be fixed and clearly governed with no casual changes, while Statement B permits priorities to be changed freely by any pricing user at any time, which directly contradicts the governance and stability requirement.

Statement A says the platform consumes only the effective winning price (implying it receives pre-determined winning prices), while Statement B says the platform receives every price candidate and selects the winning price itself (implying it makes the selection), which are contradictory responsibilities for price determination.

Statement A requires business review of prices after technical upload success, while Statement B explicitly states no further business review is needed after technical upload succeeds, making these two requirements mutually incompatible.

Statement A requires monitoring of missing cost prices as a control issue due to operational impact, while Statement B states missing cost prices have no effect on ordering and do not need monitoring, creating directly contradictory requirements for the same condition.

Statement A requires review/approval to occur before a staged promotion goes live, while Statement B requires staged promotions to go live automatically upon loading with review happening afterwards, making both conditions mutually exclusive for the same promotion workflow.

Statement A requires store intervention before printing labels, while Statement B specifies labels are printed automatically without any store intervention, making both approaches impossible to follow simultaneously for the same labels and stores.

Statement A requires downstream systems to honour promotion date ranges, while Statement B requires them to ignore these dates and apply promotions indefinitely until manual removal, creating mutually exclusive operational requirements.

Statement A requires both quantity AND value to be consumed during recipe depletion, while Statement B explicitly states value does not need to be depleted, creating incompatible requirements for the same process.

Statement A requires only affected categories to be reclassified when one category changes annually, while Statement B requires all age-restricted categories to be reclassified together when any category's threshold changes.
The two statements specify different minimum submission lead times (6 weeks vs. 3 weeks) for the same requirement, making them mutually exclusive for the same promotion.
Both statements convey identical substantive guidance: when checks fail, the process halts and the requester receives notification, differing only in wording.
Both statements convey the same substantive guidance: supplier status serves as a readiness control, and downstream processes independently prevent use of suppliers lacking mandatory contracts.
Both statements require the same two conditions (clear business owner and defined use case) for creating or retaining attributes, expressing identical substantive guidance in different wording.
Both statements convey the same substantive guidance: that article lists are flexible groupings distinct from the fixed/structural merchandise hierarchy.

Both statements establish the same substantive requirement that article lists must have a justified business purpose (usage scenario/use case) and should not be created unnecessarily, with both implicitly ruling out redundant or unjustified lists.
Both statements convey the same substantive guidance: that technical activation of an article is distinct from and does not guarantee operational readiness.
Both statements convey identical substantive guidance that cost price and sales price can be changed simultaneously through the structured upload route, using different wording.
Both statements convey the same guidance: that monitoring of promotion load success is essential because execution errors quickly become visible to customers.

Both statements convey the same substantive guidance: that article lists and grouped structures can be reused in promotions to avoid manual loading of long product sets, differing only in wording and phrasing.
Both statements require maintaining an explicit distinction between ingredient-only items and their sellable equivalents, conveying identical substantive guidance despite minor wording variations.
Both statements require testing to cover the complete ingredient journey beyond just recipe depletion in the core system, using different but equivalent wording.
Both statements convey identical substantive guidance: that annual age-threshold changes should be implemented as a repeatable process rather than handled manually on an ad hoc basis.
